extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists (graduate students, researchers, textbook/authors) writing papers, expositions, and books
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing mathematical and computer-science expositions, papers, and books aimed at both specialist and general audiences. Covers style, structure, examples, notation, publication pragmatics, and proofreading/page-proof practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make material accessible to a general reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Write (or edit) exposition to be understandable by a general audience—remove unnecessary jargon and explain concepts intuitively; be willing to reword for clarity when producing material 'edited for the general reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Don's SA paper was heavily edited to remove jargon and make it accessible; some editorial changes, even if seemingly gratuitous, can reveal where exposition was unclear. Balance technical detail with accessibility when aiming for non-specialist venues (e.g., Scientific American never displays equations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve technical and typographical accuracy in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure mathematical symbols and notation are typeset correctly and not mangled by copy-editing or typesetting processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check page proofs carefully: look for characters mistaken for others (e.g., '1' vs 'l', '∅' vs 'ϕ'), bracket/parenthesis misuse, and formula-specific conventions (floor brackets vs square brackets). Many errors only appear at page-proof stage and must be corrected then.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit and consistent about notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose notation deliberately (e.g., 'lg' to mean log base 2) and do not allow it to be changed to ambiguous alternatives (e.g., 'log') without explaining meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid notation that can be misinterpreted by other audiences (engineers, number theorists). If a publisher attempts to substitute standard but ambiguous notation, insist on clarifying or restoring your chosen symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use numerals and separators appropriate to context
rubrics_metrics.description: Format numbers according to context: in formulas prefer compact forms without locale-dependent separators; in running text follow publisher conventions (commas, spaces, or scientific notation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: author used '1000000' in formulas; ACM changed to '1,000,000'; IEEE uses spaces (e.g., '1 234 567'); publishers differ—decide what's appropriate for formulas vs text and argue during proofreading if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose voice and person thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide on first-person ('I'/'we') or impersonal voice based on audience and venue; first-person/‘we’ can be effective in exposition though some editors may change it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf endorses use of first-person in technical writing; Knuth/Don note editors sometimes replace 'we'. Use the voice that best serves clarity and reader engagement, and be prepared to defend it in edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the reader's attention immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use snappy titles, arresting first sentences, and lucid initial paragraphs to hook readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of effective attention-getting titles and openings were given (Gleason, Thurston, Taussky-Todd). Fame helps, but good openings are crucial regardless of author recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell readers up front what you will do
rubrics_metrics.description: State in plain English the goals and main results early so readers can decide whether to read on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit upfront statements can substantially increase readership ('You can quintuple your readership if you will let them in on what it is that you are doing').

rubrics_metrics.name: Make results and key statements easy to find when skimming
rubrics_metrics.description: Format and place important results so skimmers can latch on—use boldface/typographic emphasis and avoid heavy notation in theorem statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers scan looking for theorems; remove notational abbreviations and convoluted references from statement text so page-flippers can make informed decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use motivation and examples judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide some motivation and illustrative examples, but avoid excessive or repetitive motivational material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A few failed examples can be useful, but the technique loses charm after several instances. Keep motivation concise and purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include many clear examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Use examples liberally: simple examples convey most of an idea; later refine with more complex examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman: 'I never saw a book with too many examples.' Finding good examples that illustrate 'all and only' the intended points takes effort—be prepared to invest time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place definitions close to their uses and repeat when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep definitions near where they are used; do not assume readers will flip back to earlier chapters for essential definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's acceptable to repeat definitions to aid understanding; readers do not learn by jumping back and forth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match exposition level to reader capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the level of exposition accessible rather than opaque: avoid heavy machinery when it would obscure understanding for your intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tradeoff: teaching deep mechanics may require long digressions; instead, do the basic calculations/proofs and refer to other texts for deeper results if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: State types and be explicit about references
rubrics_metrics.description: State the types of variables and avoid terse non-referential expressions (e.g., avoid 'this' used ambiguously).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: say 'the set S' rather than 'S'. Ullman's English professor warned against non-referential 'this'—it confuses readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an exposition rhythm: chatty around proofs, lean in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Be conversational and motivating before and after proofs, but present proofs in a concise, rigorous ('lean and mean') style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilf prefers being 'chatty' leading up to a proof and after it, but the proof itself should be concise similar to Rudin's style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build intuition before presenting complicated algorithms/proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use puzzles or motivating examples to construct the mental structures readers need to appreciate the algorithm or proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don's technique: present an example/puzzle that makes the need for the algorithm apparent; even if the algorithm is complex, the reader will better follow the later formal presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose names and terminology carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick names for concepts and structures with awareness that names can stick and may be hard to change later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: regret over 'Daemon' vs 'Oracle', LR(k) vs L(k), 'nematocyst' vs 'stinger'. Community polls sometimes change names (e.g., NP-complete).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of editorial rewriting and know what to defend
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate copy-editors making changes (restructuring sentences, removing/adding commas, changing relative clauses, altering technical terms); defend changes that affect technical meaning or clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don's experience: editors altered 'which'/'that', changed commas, removed jargon, and sometimes introduced errors—use proofs and galley checks to catch and correct harmful edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect and correct page proofs thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat page proofs as an opportunity to catch typesetting and layout problems not visible earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix symbol conversions, bracket misuse, orphaned lines/subheading breaks, misplaced photographs, and layout-induced changes that alter meaning; request proofs if mathematics-heavy (publishers may make exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare camera-ready material and know publisher conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of and, where appropriate, prepare camera-ready copy to reduce publisher errors and to negotiate better royalties; learn and conform to publisher-specific typographic conventions unless they harm technical accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman notes CS authors can reduce publisher costs by preparing camera-ready copy, yielding leverage in royalty negotiations; still, insist on not sacrificing formula clarity to meet arbitrary style rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborate with co-authors to filter idiosyncrasies
rubrics_metrics.description: Use co-authors to catch personal oddities and improve the book/paper's clarity and marketability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-authors don't necessarily save time, but they help 'filter out your idiosyncrasies' and can make the final text more broadly acceptable (Ullman/Wilf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unethical or careless borrowing; be explicit about quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present others' expression/derivations as your own; explicit quotation and attribution are necessary when borrowing language or material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarism becomes culpable when a reasonable person would think the author copied from another source; quoting is acceptable in surveys; be cautious about copying notation/formatting that makes content look identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and metaphor where they aid understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ analogy and metaphor in exposition when confident the reader will grasp the intended intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ullman encouraged analogy in CS as long as it helps the reader; Don used biological metaphors in explaining complicated reductions (e.g., 'jellyfish' metaphor) to name parts of structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to publish: quality over quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write or publish papers for the wrong reasons (padding CVs, inserting papers in proceedings); publish only when you have done something genuinely valuable or are excited about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamport: two bad reasons to write are to lengthen a publications list or to get into a specific conference; a good reason is genuine excitement about the work. Judge whether work is worth publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of genre and audience when selecting exposition style and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Match lean/concise vs longer/chatty treatments to the publication venue (e.g., Monthly vs Journal of Algorithms) and to reader expectations (expository vs research results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journal of Algorithms: new, important, significant results—presentation beauty is secondary. The American Mathematical Monthly: expository, a home for excellent exposition. Choose approach accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use editorial emphasis to highlight human contribution appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that some editors emphasize human contributions (reordering sentences to stress people), and decide whether to accept or contest such restructurings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary-Claire noted Scientific American often stresses human contributions, sometimes at expense of the ideas—be aware of such editorial tendencies and their effect on presentation.
